source.title: The BUTTER Zone: An Empirical Study of Training Dynamics in Fully Connected Neural Networks
source.authors: C. Tripp; J. Perr-Sauer; Lucas Hayne; Monte Lunacek; Jamil Gafur

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps model size, training time, label noise, and regularization in fully connected MLPs and reports results relevant to double descent, using its own tasks and experimental setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own size- and epoch-wise test-loss results and its own investigations of label noise and regularization. Results cited from prior studies are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: A dataset survey of fully connected MLPs on 13 tabular tasks. It sweeps parameter count by epoch and explicitly probes for model-wise and epoch-wise double descent, including Nakkiran-style label noise, and reports qualitative outcomes. This is a new setting (MLPs, tabular data, Adam) rather than a reproduction of the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The paper is primarily a dataset release. On double descent, the authors report that larger networks generalize better even well beyond the interpolation threshold, and that there are hints of epoch-wise double descent at high parameter counts (depth 8). Longer training, larger nets and label noise did not show strong evidence of epoch-wise double descent, and regularization did not induce it.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures test performance across model size and training epochs and varies label noise and regularization, but uses a large MLP dataset spanning 13 tabular tasks and many architecture and hyperparameter settings rather than an explicit reproduction of the original experimental settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported patterns vary with parameter count, depth, task, label noise, and regularization. The depth-8, high-parameter-count setting is specifically cited for hints of epoch-wise double descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Relative run-to-run variation (IQR/median) of test loss is high around the interpolation threshold; networks sometimes learn faster or slower there regardless of optimizer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Seed-to-seed variance of test loss peaks near the interpolation threshold in MLPs.

fits_no_version.finding: Empirical fits: log parameter count is linear in the inverse cube root of the minimizing epoch, and minimum test loss follows a power law in parameter count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MLPs, the optimal stopping epoch and minimum test loss scale predictably with parameter count.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The reported double-descent conclusions are mainly qualitative; the paper says the epoch-wise evidence is not strong. The analysis uses fully connected MLPs on a finite set of tabular tasks and hyperparameter combinations, and the authors note that their preliminary analysis uses only a fraction of the dataset.
record.rows_left_out: Individual task-by-task curves and parameter-specific values in Figures 3 and 9-28 are not extracted as separate rows because the text does not state their numerical values; the reported aggregate qualitative findings are recorded above.

untested.parts: Existence and location of a test-error peak near the interpolation threshold, measured with final rather than early-stopped test loss.
All; the empirical fits relate parameter count to minimizing epoch and minimum loss, not to an effective-complexity measure of peak location.
Triple or multiple descent; removal of an existing peak by optimally tuned regularization; noise dependence of a model-wise peak.

missing.what: Optimizer Sweep: SGD has a flatter low-loss region beyond the interpolation threshold, with milder decreases in minimizing epoch as size grows.
L1 and L2 regularization 'reduced or eliminated overtraining' across visualized tasks; relevant context for V6 regularization but not a peak removal.

record.verdict_notes: All double-descent evidence is qualitative, read from contour plots, with no numeric curves. The interpolation threshold is mentioned but never located numerically. R1 uses minimum-over-epochs test loss, which matters for interpreting the absence of a model-wise peak. The V2 challenge rests on the authors' explicit statement, not on numbers.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report a numeric fall-rise-fall curve or establish the precise location of a peak relative to the interpolation threshold.
The paper reports qualitative evidence rather than numeric epoch-wise curves for the cited conditions.
The study does not sweep the number of training samples near the interpolation threshold.
The experiments use fully connected MLPs only; they do not test the claim across model classes.
The paper fits empirical relationships involving parameter count and epoch, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
The study varies label noise and regularization but does not test triple or multiple descent, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes an existing peak.
The study does not compare parameter counts with an alternative effective-parameter measure to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: FC MLPs in the Primary Sweep
rows.operation_detail: Swept parameter count and measured median minimum test loss.
rows.measure: Median minimum test loss as a function of parameter count
rows.value: The authors report that larger networks performed better, including well beyond the interpolation threshold.
rows.uncertainty: Interquartile range is shown in the marginal plots; no numerical uncertainty for this result is stated.
rows.note: This reports improved generalization at larger sizes, but does not establish the full fall-rise-fall shape or a peak near interpolation.
rows.check: The measure is median minimum test loss over 3k epochs, which is effectively early stopping and can suppress a model-wise peak. The second descent (larger nets better beyond interpolation) is reported, but no peak is reported and the threshold is not located numerically.

conditions.value: increasing levels; exact values not stated here

rows.measure: Epoch-wise test loss and evidence of epoch-wise double descent
rows.value: The authors report that the Label Noise Sweep did not show strong evidence of epoch-wise double descent; high label noise degraded performance.
rows.uncertainty: Interquartile range is shown in the plots; no numerical uncertainty for this result is stated.
rows.note: The reported label-noise effect on performance is qualitative and varies by task; the paper does not report that noise creates a clear epoch-wise double-descent peak.
rows.check: Label noise of 0 to 0.2 was added specifically to trigger epoch-wise double descent, as suggested by Nakkiran, and it did not produce strong evidence of it. Degraded performance under noise is not a peak.

rows.operation_detail: Varied L1 and L2 kernel regularization penalties.

conditions.value: 14 levels of L1 and 14 levels of L2 regularization

rows.measure: Test loss and presence of deep double descent under regularization
rows.value: The authors state that regularization did not induce deep double descent in their experiments; heavy regularization could delay the onset and reduce the severity of overtraining.
rows.uncertainty: Interquartile range is shown in the plots; no numerical uncertainty for this result is stated.
rows.note: The study varies regularization, but does not establish whether optimally tuned regularization removes an existing peak.
rows.check: V6 says tuned regularization removes an existing peak. Here there was no peak to remove, and the finding 'regularization did not induce DD' is not what V6 predicts or forbids. L1/L2 'reduced or eliminated overtraining', but overtraining is not a double-descent peak.

tranche.reason: The study directly probes double descent in a new setting: fully connected MLPs on varied PMLB tasks, using architecture, training-duration, and noise sweeps.

source_check.notes: The source is the October 2023 v2 text of the 2022 arXiv submission. Minimum test loss over training is an oracle test-set selection measure; the unsuccessful epoch-wise sweeps are qualitative non-findings, without numerical peak estimates.

statements.correction: Table II: noise levels range from 0 to 0.2. Section IV-A: classification uses label permutation; regression uses additive Gaussian noise with standard deviation proportional to the response variable's standard deviation. All three additional sweeps lack strong evidence of epoch-wise double descent; the Primary Sweep supplies hints at depth 8 and high parameter counts.
statements.problem: The findings and noise bound are correct, but a label-noise fraction does not describe the intervention uniformly across classification and regression tasks.
